clinicalPearls: A focal disorder of subchondral bone and overlying articular cartilage that may separate as an osteochondral fragment, distinct from a diffuse osteonecrosis or apophysitis
Most commonly affects the knee, classically the lateral aspect of the medial femoral condyle, and also the capitellum and the talar dome
Occurs in adolescents and young adults; juvenile disease with open physes generally has a better prognosis than adult-onset disease
Presents with poorly localised activity-related joint pain, and with mechanical symptoms such as catching, locking or giving way once a fragment becomes unstable
The radiographic hallmark is a crescentic radiolucent line demarcating an osteochondral fragment from the underlying bone
Fragment stability is the central determinant of management and prognosis and is best assessed on magnetic resonance imaging
A stable lesion with intact overlying cartilage may heal with offloading, whereas an unstable fragment or a loose body usually requires surgery
Management spans activity modification and immobilisation for stable juvenile lesions through to fixation, drilling or fragment removal and cartilage restoration as needed
reference.pathophysiology: Osteochondritis dissecans is a focal disturbance of the subchondral bone in which a segment of bone and its overlying articular cartilage may lose structural continuity with the parent bone. Although the precise cause is debated, repetitive microtrauma and localised ischaemia of the subchondral bone are thought to be central, sometimes with a contribution from disordered ossification of the epiphysis in the growing skeleton. The affected subchondral bone weakens and a demarcation line develops; if the overlying cartilage remains intact the lesion may be stable and heal, but progressive separation can leave the fragment partially attached (a flap) or fully detached as an intra-articular loose body. Once the fragment is unstable the articular surface becomes incongruent, causing mechanical symptoms and predisposing to secondary degenerative change.
additionalDifferentials: Chondral (cartilage) injury without a bony fragment
Loose body from another cause such as synovial chondromatosis
In the elbow, capitellar Panner disease in a younger child
additionalInvestigations: Plain radiographs including tunnel or notch views to detect the crescentic lucency and any loose body
Magnetic resonance imaging to assess cartilage integrity and stage fragment stability
Assessment for fluid tracking behind the fragment on imaging as a sign of instability
Computed tomography to define the bony bed when planning surgery
Examination for a joint effusion, mechanical symptoms and localised tenderness
Comparison with the contralateral joint and evaluation of physeal status
redFlags: Mechanical locking or a palpable loose body indicating an unstable, detached fragment
A recurrent tense effusion suggesting an unstable lesion or intra-articular derangement
Progressive articular surface collapse or established secondary arthritis
Adult-onset disease with a large lesion carrying a higher risk of poor healing
reference.prognosis: Stable lesions in skeletally immature patients often heal with conservative management, whereas unstable fragments, loose bodies and adult-onset lesions have a poorer capacity to heal and carry an increased long-term risk of osteoarthritis if the articular surface is not restored.
pitfalls: Assuming a lesion is stable without magnetic resonance imaging assessment of the overlying cartilage
Missing a detached loose body as a cause of intermittent locking
Confusing capitellar disease in a young child (Panner disease) with adolescent osteochondritis dissecans
Under-treating an unstable fragment and allowing progressive articular damage
management: Non-operative treatment of stable lesions in skeletally immature patients with activity restriction, protected weight-bearing and sometimes bracing to promote healing across the open physis
Antegrade or retrograde subchondral drilling of a stable juvenile lesion that fails to heal with rest
Arthroscopic fixation of an unstable but salvageable fragment, with removal of loose bodies
Cartilage restoration by microfracture, osteochondral autograft or allograft transplantation, or autologous chondrocyte implantation for detached or unsalvageable fragments
Monitoring of healing with serial imaging and staged return to activity
Long-term surveillance for osteoarthritis, with referral to orthopaedics for unstable, adult-onset or failed lesions
